text: The OSSL database description describes the OSSL variables and their column names.

title: OSSL datasets
text:
The OSSL container


source

OSSL
def OSSL(
    df:pandas.DataFrame, # OSSL data, one row per sample
):
OSSL (Open Soil Spectral Library) data container, indexed by sample ID


OSSL indexes its DataFrame by sample ID (id), using the id.layer_uuid_txt column. The OSSL documentation names this column as the key for joining OSSL tables. Every row has a distinct value.
OSSL passes any attribute it doesn’t define to its DataFrame, through fastcore’s GetAttr. So ossl.loc, ossl.columns and the other DataFrame attributes work directly on ossl. Indexing with a column name or a list of names returns those columns, as in pandas. Indexing with anything else, such as a boolean mask, returns a new OSSL with the selected samples.
The local ID id.layer_local_c is not unique. In OSSL v1.2, 82 local IDs appear in two source datasets. For example, 1002 identifies one sample in CAF.SSL and another in KSSL.SSL. Joining on the local ID pairs the spectra of one sample with the properties of the other. To see the local ID and its source dataset, select them with ossl[['id.layer_local_c', 'dataset.code_ascii_txt']].

title: OSSL datasets
text:
Loading the data


source

get_cache_path
def get_cache_path(
    dest_dir:str='.soilspecdata', # Name of the cache directory, relative to the home directory
)->pathlib.Path: # Path to the cache directory
Get cache path for OSSL data


The cache directory is ~/.soilspecdata by default:

get_cache_path()

Path('/Users/franckalbinet/.soilspecdata')


load_ossl downloads the whole OSSL v1.2 database as one gzipped CSV file. OSSL publishes it at two data levels:

L0 (the default, ossl_all_L0_v1.2.csv.gz) keeps the lab method of each source dataset. The same property can have one column per method, such as cec_usda.a723_cmolc.kg and cec_iso.11260_cmolc.kg.
L1 (ossl_all_L1_v1.2.csv.gz) converts properties measured with different methods to one target method. It has 24 fewer property columns than L0, for example no cec_iso.11260_cmolc.kg.

Both levels have the same spectra and ID columns. load_ossl caches the file under its own name, in the directory from get_cache_path. Each level or url therefore has its own cache file.


source

load_ossl
def load_ossl(
    level:str='L0', # OSSL data level: 'L0' (original lab methods) or 'L1' (lab methods converted to a target method)
    url:NoneType=None, # OSSL gzipped CSV URL; if None, the whole-database file for `level`
    force_download:bool=False, # if True, download even if the file is cached
)->__main__.OSSL:
Load OSSL data from the cache, downloading it first if needed


Load the default L0 data, from the cache if it is there:

ossl = load_ossl()

title: OSSL datasets
text:
Columns
OSSL sorts the columns into VISNIR spectra (visnir_cols), MIR spectra (mir_cols) and all other columns (meta_cols). The other columns hold soil properties, site data and metadata:

ossl.visnir_cols[:2], ossl.mir_cols[:2], ossl.meta_cols[:2]

(['scan_visnir.350_ref', 'scan_visnir.352_ref'],
 ['scan_mir.600_abs', 'scan_mir.602_abs'],
 ['dataset.code_ascii_txt', 'id.layer_local_c'])


meta_cols has 133 columns in v1.2. Soil-lab column names follow the pattern <property>_<method>_<unit>. For example, cec_usda.a723_cmolc.kg is the cation exchange capacity (CEC), measured with USDA method A723, in cmolc/kg. To find the columns for one property, filter on its name:

[c for c in ossl.meta_cols if c.startswith('cec')]

['cec_iso.11260_cmolc.kg', 'cec_usda.a723_cmolc.kg']


The same property can have several methods. The methods come from USDA or ISO standards, aqua regia extraction (aquaregia) or Mehlich-3 extraction (mel3). The table below counts the soil-lab columns of each property by standard. It leaves out the ISO 8601 date columns and the ISO 3166 country column, which use ISO formats rather than lab methods:

lab = pd.Series(ossl.meta_cols).str.extract(r'^(?P<property>[^_]+)_(?P<method>(?:usda|iso)\.\w+|aquaregia|mel3)_').dropna()
lab = lab[~lab.method.isin(['iso.8601', 'iso.3166'])]
pd.crosstab(lab.property, lab.method.str.split('.').str[0])

title: OSSL datasets
text:
Selecting samples
Filter samples with ordinary pandas conditions on the columns of ossl. The result is an OSSL with the selected samples, so every method in this notebook works on it. The KSSL samples only:

kssl = ossl[ossl['dataset.code_ascii_txt'] == 'KSSL.SSL']
test_eq(set(kssl['dataset.code_ascii_txt']), {'KSSL.SSL'})
len(kssl), len(ossl)

(86603, 135651)


Conditions combine with & and |. US samples whose layer starts less than 30 cm below the surface:

us_top = ossl[(ossl['location.country_iso.3166_txt'] == 'USA') & (ossl['layer.upper.depth_usda_cm'] < 30)]
len(us_top)

52214

OSSL._extract_wavenumbers
def _extract_wavenumbers(
    cols:List[str], # Spectral column names
)->numpy.ndarray: # Wavenumbers in cm⁻¹
Wavenumbers of spectral columns, converting VISNIR wavelengths in nm to wavenumbers


MIR column names give the wavenumber in cm⁻¹, as in scan_mir.600_abs. VISNIR column names give the wavelength in nm, as in scan_visnir.350_ref. _extract_wavenumbers converts wavelengths to wavenumbers (10⁷/λ, rounded to the nearest integer), so every method of OSSL works in wavenumbers. The 350 nm VISNIR column becomes 28571 cm⁻¹:

ossl.mir_cols[0], ossl._extract_wavenumbers(ossl.mir_cols)[0], ossl.visnir_cols[0], ossl._extract_wavenumbers(ossl.visnir_cols)[0]

('scan_mir.600_abs', np.int64(600), 'scan_visnir.350_ref', np.int64(28571))




source

OSSL._extract_measurement_type
def _extract_measurement_type(
    cols:List[str], # Spectral column names
)->str: # `abs` (absorbance) or `ref` (reflectance)
Extract measurement type from column names


The suffix of the column names gives the measurement type. OSSL reports VISNIR spectra as reflectance and MIR spectra as absorbance:

ossl._extract_measurement_type(ossl.visnir_cols), ossl._extract_measurement_type(ossl.mir_cols)

('ref', 'abs')

OSSL._filter_wavenumbers
def _filter_wavenumbers(
    wavenumbers:numpy.ndarray, # Wavenumbers of `cols`
    cols:List[str], # Spectral column names
    wmin:Optional[int]=None, # Min wavenumber; the smallest in `wavenumbers` if None
    wmax:Optional[int]=None, # Max wavenumber; the largest in `wavenumbers` if None
)->Tuple[numpy.ndarray, List[str]]: # Wavenumbers and column names within the range
Wavenumbers and columns between wmin and wmax, inclusive


The VISNIR columns are in order of increasing wavelength. Their wavenumbers therefore decrease. Between 4000 and 25000 cm⁻¹, the VISNIR columns run from 400 nm (25000 cm⁻¹) to 2500 nm (4000 cm⁻¹):

wavenumbers, cols = ossl._filter_wavenumbers(ossl._extract_wavenumbers(ossl.visnir_cols), ossl.visnir_cols, wmin=4000, wmax=25000)
wavenumbers.min(), wavenumbers.max(), cols[0], cols[-1]

title: SoilSpecData
text:
Load the Open Soil Spectral Library (OSSL) as spectra and soil properties ready for machine learning.
OSSL is an open database of soil spectra, with the lab-measured soil properties of the same samples. Version 1.2 combines 10 spectral libraries, from the US KSSL library (86,603 samples) and the European LUCAS survey (40,175) to smaller regional ones. It holds 135,651 samples, with mid-infrared (MIR) spectra for 85,684 of them and visible and near-infrared (VISNIR) spectra for 64,644. OSSL publishes the whole database as one CSV file of about 1 GB.
SoilSpecData downloads and caches that file, and gives the spectra in wavenumbers. It aligns spectra with soil properties by sample. One line then gives you X and y for a model. The OSSL documentation describes the database and how OSSL builds it.
The SoilSpecData documentation covers the full API.

title: SoilSpecData
text:
Installation
pip install -U soilspecdata
To install the development version, with the development tools nbdev and twine, run this in the project root:
pip install -e .[dev]

title: SoilSpecData
text:
Features

Download and cache the OSSL database, at data level L0 or L1
VISNIR (visible and near-infrared) and MIR (mid-infrared) spectra, in wavenumbers, for any wavenumber range
Soil properties and metadata as pandas DataFrames, indexed by sample ID
Spectra and target variables aligned by sample, ready for machine learning
Further datasets to come …

title: SoilSpecData
text:
Quick start
from soilspecdata.all import * imports load_ossl, OSSL, Spectra and get_cache_path. Each also has its own module, such as soilspecdata.datasets.ossl, for explicit imports. Load OSSL, then get the MIR spectra and CEC values of every sample that has both. The first call downloads about 1 GB. Later calls read the cached file instead. Loading took 24 seconds on an Apple silicon Mac. Memory use peaks at about 12 GB while pandas reads the file. The loaded data then takes 3.5 GB:

from soilspecdata.all import *


ossl = load_ossl()


X, y, ids = ossl.mir().xy('cec_usda.a723_cmolc.kg')
X.shape, y.shape

((57062, 1701), (57062, 1))

title: SoilSpecData
text:
Loading the data
load_ossl() loads the L0 data. L0 keeps the lab method of each source dataset. load_ossl(level='L1') loads the L1 data. L1 converts properties measured with different lab methods to one target method.
load_ossl caches each downloaded file in ~/.soilspecdata/, under the file’s own name, such as ossl_all_L0_v1.2.csv.gz. To download the file again:
ossl = load_ossl(force_download=True)

title: SoilSpecData
text:
Spectra
OSSL MIR spectra cover 600 to 4000 cm⁻¹. VISNIR spectra cover 350 to 2500 nm, or 4000 to 28571 cm⁻¹. mir and visnir return both in wavenumbers, in increasing order. They return only the samples with a value at every wavenumber in the range.
Their wmin and wmax parameters select a wavenumber range. By default, mir returns 600 to 4000 cm⁻¹, which covers all 85,684 MIR spectra. By default, visnir returns 4000 to 25000 cm⁻¹ (400 to 2500 nm). That range covers all 64,644 VISNIR spectra. Only 23,880 of them start at 350 nm.
The MIR spectra over the default range:

mir_data = ossl.mir()

The VISNIR spectra between 8000 and 25000 cm⁻¹:

visnir_data = ossl.visnir(wmin=8000, wmax=25000)

Both methods return a Spectra, with these fields:

wavenumbers: wavenumbers in cm⁻¹, in increasing order
spectra: one row per sample, one column per wavenumber
measurement_type: ref (reflectance) or abs (absorbance)
sample_ids: the sample ID of each row

Printing a Spectra shows the start of each field:

print(visnir_data)

Any column in ossl.meta_cols can serve as a target or as metadata. Soil-lab column names follow the pattern <property>_<method>_<unit>. title: SoilSpecData
text:
Upgrading from 0.0.x
Version 0.1.0 changed the API. To update code written for version 0.0.x:

get_ossl(url, force_download, level) is now load_ossl(level, url, force_download).
get_mir and get_visnir are now mir and visnir.
ossl.get_aligned_data(spectra, targets) is now spectra.xy(targets).
ossl.get_properties(cols) is now ossl[cols]. Add .dropna() for require_complete=True.
OSSLData, SpectraData and properties_cols are now OSSL, Spectra and meta_cols.
ossl.df is indexed by sample ID (id.layer_uuid_txt) instead of by row number.

Version 0.1.0 still accepted the old names. Version 0.2.0 removes them. If your code runs on 0.1.0 without a DeprecationWarning, and doesn’t use OSSLData, SpectraData, properties_cols or get_properties, it runs on 0.2.0 unchanged.

def Spectra(
    wavenumbers:numpy.ndarray, spectra:numpy.ndarray, measurement_type:str, sample_ids:numpy.ndarray,
    source:object=None
)->None:
Spectra of several samples, measured at the same wavenumbers




Exported source
from dataclasses import dataclass, field, fields
import numpy as np




Exported source
@dataclass
class Spectra:
    "Spectra of several samples, measured at the same wavenumbers"
    wavenumbers:np.ndarray # Wavenumbers in cm⁻¹, in increasing order
    spectra:np.ndarray # One row per sample, one column per wavenumber
    measurement_type:str # `abs` (absorbance) or `ref` (reflectance)
    sample_ids:np.ndarray # Sample ID of each row of `spectra`
    source:object=field(default=None, repr=False, compare=False) # Object the spectra came from, such as an `OSSL`

    def __str__(self):
        'Pretty print the Spectra object'
        sections = [
            ("Spectra attributes", f"Available attributes: {', '.join(f.name for f in fields(self) if f.repr)}"),
            
            ("Wavenumbers", 
                f"{np.array2string(self.wavenumbers[:10], precision=2, separator=', ')}\n"
                f"Shape: {self.wavenumbers.shape}"),
            
            ("Spectra", 
                f"{np.array2string(self.spectra[:5,:5], precision=4, separator=', ')}\n"
                f"Shape: {self.spectra.shape}"),
            
            ("Measurement type (Reflectance or Absorbance)", self.measurement_type),
            
            ("Sample IDs", 
                f"{np.array2string(self.sample_ids[:10], separator=', ')}\n"
                f"Total samples: {len(self.sample_ids)}")]
        
        return '\n\n'.join(f"{title}:\n{'-'*len(title)}\n{content}" 
            for title, content in sections)


OSSL.get_mir and OSSL.get_visnir return a Spectra. Row i of spectra is the spectrum of sample sample_ids[i], measured at wavenumbers. Printing a Spectra shows the start of each field and its shape. Two MIR spectra at three wavenumbers:

sd = Spectra(np.array([600, 602, 604]), np.array([[0.11, 0.12, 0.13], [0.21, 0.22, 0.23]]), 'abs', np.array(['s1', 's2']))
print(sd)
